Count the Collatz steps that take a positive integer to 1.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/collatz-conjecture) (MIT). Listed under [Numbers & Math](/examples/?subject=numbers-and-math).

```nomi-run
// FILE: collatz_conjecture.nomi
/// How many Collatz steps take `number` to 1: halve an even number, and
/// triple an odd one and add 1.
pub fn steps(number: Int) -> Result<Int, String> {
    if number < 1 {
        return Err("Only positive integers are allowed")
    }

    Iter.iterate(number, next)
    |> Iter.take_while(&(&1 != 1))
    |> Iter.count()
    |> Ok()
}

fn next(n: Int) -> Int {
    if n % 2 == 0 { n / 2 } else { 3 * n + 1 }
}

// FILE: collatz_conjecture_test.nomi
import collatz_conjecture

test "counts the steps" {
    cases = [
        #("zero steps for one", 1, 0),
        #("divide if even", 16, 4),
        #("even and odd steps", 12, 9),
        #("large number of even and odd steps", 1000000, 152),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, number, expected), description {
        assert collatz_conjecture.steps(number) == Ok(expected)
    }
}

test "zero is an error" {
    assert collatz_conjecture.steps(0) == Err("Only positive integers are allowed")
}

test "negative value is an error" {
    assert collatz_conjecture.steps(-15) == Err("Only positive integers are allowed")
}
```

## How it's written

- The sequence is `Iter.iterate(number, next)`, cut at the first 1 with `Iter.take_while(&(&1 != 1))` and counted. That states the problem directly; a tail-recursive counter was the other option. The cut is one comparison, so it is written as the capture `&(&1 != 1)` rather than as `fn n -> n != 1`.
- A non-positive input returns `Err` with the canonical message, through an early `return` before the pipeline.
- The four step counts are a `subtests` table; the two error cases are plain tests, since they assert a different shape.
